The African sharptooth catfish relative, Vundu (Heterobranchus longifilis), is one of the largest freshwater teleosts on the continent, with a documented maximum adult body mass of 55,000 grams [Wwi = 55,000 grams] and an ultimate total length reaching 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters] in the wild. Field surveys and growth studies consistently report that individuals can achieve this impressive size, though exceptional specimens have been recorded at 180 cm and 45.5 kg, underscoring the species' considerable growth potential. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' preferred deep-water habitats at 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was measured at 7.7% [GSI = 7.7%]. This relatively low value is consistent with patterns observed in other large-bodied siluriforms that exhibit protracted growth and delayed reproductive investment.

Early life history in Vundu begins with the deposition of small, demersal, adhesive eggs that are approximately 1.4 mm in diameter. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva bears a wet weight at birth of 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the diminutive size of the incubation products. The duration of the pre-feeding, endotrophic phase is highly dependent on ambient water temperature. In comparative rearing trials that draw on values from the closely related Clarias gariepinus, the age at birth, defined as the interval between egg fertilisation and chorion rupture, was observed to be 1.25 days [ab = 1.25 days] when embryos were incubated at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. In contrast, when incubation temperatures were elevated to 33 °C [T = 33 °C], the age at birth was substantially shorter, requiring only 0.58 days [ab = 0.58 days] for hatching to occur. This rapid developmental response to thermal variation is a common adaptation among tropical siluriforms inhabiting seasonally variable floodplain environments.

Juvenile Vundu undergo a period of rapid somatic growth following the transition to exogenous feeding, during which they are voracious piscivores. The species reaches the onset of gonadal maturation and physiological puberty at a wet weight of approximately 700 grams [Wwp = approximately 700 grams]. Individuals attaining this body mass are considered reproductively viable, although first spawning in natural populations may be delayed until a larger size is achieved, depending on local resource availability and population density. The wet weight at puberty of 700 grams [Wwp = 700 grams] represents a substantial threshold, equivalent to only about 1.3 percent of the ultimate adult wet weight, indicating that the species invests considerable energy in early growth before diverting resources toward gametogenesis. This pattern of deferred maturation is characteristic of large, long-lived freshwater predators that must achieve a size sufficient to dominate prey resources and avoid gape-limited predators before committing to annual reproductive effort.

Longevity estimates for Heterobranchus longifilis indicate a considerable maximum lifespan in the wild. Under the thermal regime of their native river systems, which typically average around 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C] in the deeper pools they inhabit during the dry season, the species is known to survive for approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years]. This lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] is consistent with values reported for other large-bodied claroteid catfishes, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances relatively slow somatic growth with iteroparous annual spawning events at a temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. The protracted lifespan allows individuals to accumulate the substantial body mass required to reach reproductive maturity and to spawn repeatedly over multiple breeding seasons, thereby maximising lifetime reproductive output in an environment where annual recruitment may be highly variable due to fluctuating flood regimes and prey availability.

The reproductive ecology of Vundu is closely tied to seasonal flood pulses in large African river systems such as the Congo and Niger basins. Spawning typically occurs at the onset of the rainy season when rising water levels inundate floodplain habitats, providing nursery areas with abundant zooplankton for the exogenously feeding larvae.
